narrate.summary: The paper introduces SIGMA (Symmetry-aware, Intelligent, Geometric, Multi-faced Adaptive Traffic Control), a traffic-signal controller that combines reinforcement learning with a large language model (LLM) to respond to changing priorities such as emergency routes. It optimizes emergency response, traffic pressure, waiting-time fairness, and predictable signal transitions, while using rotated training examples to improve transfer across equivalent intersection orientations. The method is pretrained on synthetic traffic and then adapted online; evaluations use Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO), with demand calibrated from traffic observations at four intersections in Kolkata, India. The authors also examine fallback behavior when the LLM fails and use bootstrap intervals to estimate emergency service levels. In the reported simulations, the controller improves several traffic and emergency measures over fixed-time, actuated, and deep Q-Network (DQN) controllers, but the Kolkata comparison disables its emergency-priority component and is still simulation-based.
narrate.key_results: In the paper’s 1,000-episode comparison, SIGMA reports an average vehicle waiting time of 77.54 seconds, average emergency waiting time of 23.47 seconds, average queue length of 11.38, and throughput of 9.26 vehicles per interval. Compared with the DQN controller, these correspond to lower average waiting time (86.29 seconds), emergency waiting time (29.55 seconds), and queue length (13.0), and higher throughput (8.07); its average maximum waiting time was higher, at 133.27 seconds versus 121.78 seconds. At the 60-second emergency-wait threshold, the estimated service level was 0.992 for the full controller, compared with 0.847 for the queue-and-waiting-time fallback, 0.712 for DQN, and 0.341 for fixed-time control. In the four Kolkata SUMO evaluations, the emergency-free SIGMA variant had lower average delay, maximum waiting time, and queue length than the Max-Pressure comparison at every intersection; reported comparisons against PressLight were significant for maximum waiting time at all four intersections, while significance for other metrics varied by intersection.

key_equations.name: Weighted actor training objective
key_equations.explanation: The actor loss is the sum of the supervised loss and the weighted utility losses; lambda is the vector of objective weights, and the utility-loss vector contains the losses for the controller’s operational objectives.

key_equations.name: Expected performance with language-model failures
key_equations.explanation: J_mix is expected performance under simulated failures, p_fail is the failure probability, J_full is performance with the full controller, and J_QW is performance with the fallback controller.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that language-model inference latency is relatively high, at approximately 1.18 seconds. The experiments cover individual intersections, rely on a fourfold symmetry assumption for rotation augmentation, omit objectives such as emissions and pedestrian waiting, and evaluate the method in simulation rather than live traffic.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The emergency scenarios come from a predefined library, and the Kolkata evaluations turn off emergency prioritization, so emergency response is not validated against observed emergency-vehicle operations. The offline critic also approximates successor states using nearest neighbours because the dataset does not provide continuous trajectories, which may introduce value-estimation error; the paper does not quantify that error in the reported comparisons.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose reducing language-model latency through smaller models, distillation, or compression; extending the controller to coordinated networks of intersections; and generalizing symmetry-aware learning to other intersection geometries. They also propose adding objectives such as emissions, fuel use, pedestrian waiting, and public-transport priority, and testing the system with live traffic data and real-world control environments.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess reliability under sensor errors, communication delays, and correlated component outages, rather than only the simulated language-model failure process. They could also test explicit safety constraints for phase selection and report uncertainty in performance differences across repeated runs and demand conditions.

narrate.summary: The paper develops LR3, a one-parameter model for positive lifetimes that mixes an exponential distribution with a gamma distribution of shape four. The mixture weight and both component rates are linked to the same parameter, so the model is parsimonious but imposes restrictions on component proportions and durations. The authors derive distributional, reliability, density-shape, hazard, and estimation properties, and give a likelihood for independent right-censored observations. Its numerical evaluation uses generated, complete lifetime samples rather than observed field data. The hazard initially decreases for every positive parameter, and eventually increases when the gamma component governs the tail.
narrate.key_results: The simulation used 500 generated datasets in each of eight settings, for 4,000 datasets total, with sample sizes of 50 and 200 and parameter values of 0.3, 0.5, 1, and 2. Increasing sample size reduced the reported root mean squared error for both maximum likelihood and moment estimation in every setting; maximum likelihood had lower error in five of the eight settings. For parameter 2 and sample size 50, the root mean squared errors were 0.1418 for maximum likelihood and 0.2177 for moment estimation; for sample size 200, they were 0.0741 and 0.1013. The reported coverage of nominal 95% intervals ranged from 0.922 to 0.966; all likelihood fits converged successfully and all fitted observed-information values were positive. These are results under correct model specification, not comparisons against other lifetime distributions or evidence from field data.

key_equations.name: LR3 lifetime density
key_equations.explanation: Here f is the lifetime density, x is a positive lifetime, and theta is the positive model parameter; the two terms represent the exponential and shape-four gamma components.

key_equations.name: Mean lifetime
key_equations.explanation: Here mu is the mean lifetime and theta is the positive model parameter; the mean decreases strictly as theta increases.

narrate.limitations_stated: The linked component rates and mixture weight can impose an unrealistic relationship between component frequency and duration, and the fixed gamma shape of four is a modeling choice rather than a finding from observed data. The simulation covers complete, independent, correctly specified samples and a finite parameter grid; it does not establish robustness to censoring, dependence, rounding, or misspecification. The model is tied to a fixed working time unit and is not closed under arbitrary changes of time units.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper does not assess how well the model represents lifetimes when operating conditions or measured covariates vary across units; its estimation and simulation framework treats observations as identically distributed. It also does not connect the fitted component mixture to system-level failure consequences or maintenance decisions, so the reliability summaries alone do not establish the value of the model for a particular engineering decision.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose evaluating a scale extension, relaxing the fixed gamma shape, and assessing censoring and empirical performance using appropriately documented datasets. They also identify a full classification of hazard turning points as further work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could incorporate operating-condition covariates and dependence between units, then validate predictions on field data collected under those conditions. They could also connect lifetime estimates to system-level reliability and maintenance decisions, while checking whether the mixture components have a useful engineering interpretation.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses systems in which multiple performance characteristics degrade together, so failure occurs when any characteristic reaches its threshold. It models each characteristic's degradation as the sum of an individual Gamma process and a shared environmental-damage process, with a shared random effect to represent differences among units. The authors derive system reliability, estimate model parameters using an expectation-maximization procedure with variational inference, and optimize age-based preventive replacement. They evaluate the methods with simulations and accelerated-weathering measurements from four epoxy-coating specimens under one experimental condition. The proposed model estimates reliability more accurately than simplified models that omit unit heterogeneity or shared degradation, and its maintenance policy lowers the reported long-run cost rate for the coating example.
narrate.key_results: In simulation, the average relative root mean squared error for mean-time-to-failure estimates was 6.1061 × 10^-2 for the proposed model, compared with 28.8832 × 10^-2 when unit-level random effects were omitted and 21.3087 × 10^-2 when both dependence sources were omitted. For the heterogeneity parameters, relative biases were about 0.400 to 0.48 with 10 units and fell below 0.08 with 50 units. In the coating application, estimated mean time to failure was 75.3126 days; the estimated characteristic correlations ranged from 0.5133 to 0.7625 conditional on the random effect. With preventive replacement cost set to 1 and failure replacement cost set to 5, the optimal replacement time was 49.5875 days, with reliability about 0.9685 and a minimum long-run cost rate of 0.0228, versus 0.0664 for replacement only after failure—a reported reduction of about 65.7%.

key_equations.explanation: Here, Y_k(t) is total degradation for characteristic k at time t, X_k(t) is its individual component, Z(t) is shared degradation, lambda is the shared random effect, eta_k(t) and eta_0(t) are the individual and shared shape functions, and omega and rho parameterize the Gamma distribution of lambda.

key_equations.name: Threshold-based system reliability

key_equations.name: Long-run replacement cost rate

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the shared degradation process affects all characteristics with the same loading, which may be restrictive when characteristics have different sensitivities to environmental damage. They also identify measurement error, operating covariates, heterogeneous initial degradation, and random degradation onset times as features not included in the current model.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The coating analysis uses only four specimens from a single controlled accelerated-weathering condition, so it provides limited evidence about performance across other conditions or actual field service. The analysis also assumes independent units and uses a factorized variational approximation for latent quantities; the paper does not report a validation against field failure outcomes or an assessment of uncertainty from those assumptions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose adding characteristic-specific loadings or multiple shared Gamma factors to represent different sensitivities to environmental damage. They also propose incorporating measurement error, operating covariates, heterogeneous initial degradation, and random degradation onset times, and extending age replacement to condition-based or dynamically updated maintenance that accounts for inspection costs, imperfect maintenance, downtime, and uncertainty in thresholds and costs.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the model and its maintenance recommendations on longer-term field data and across multiple operating environments, including checks of how accelerated-test conditions translate to service conditions. Also study how uncertainty in estimated reliability and dependence affects replacement decisions when the unit-level sample is small.

narrate.summary: This paper studies maintenance decisions for repairable systems whose successive inter-failure times may shorten or lengthen over cycles. It models this pattern with a geometric process and develops a method to quantify uncertainty in model parameters, cycle-specific reliability and hazard, and the age at which to replace the system. It also tests whether exponential, gamma, and Weibull baseline distributions can be distinguished in finite samples. The method is evaluated with simulations and with aircraft air-conditioning failure records, focusing on one aircraft with 27 inter-failure times. The main finding is that early-cycle replacement ages can be highly uncertain: several ages may have similar expected cost while implying substantially different reliability and risk.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with sample sizes of 10, 20, and 30, the proposed generalized confidence intervals had coverage close to the nominal 95% for model parameters and cycle-specific reliability measures; bootstrap and Bayesian intervals showed undercoverage in several settings. The baseline discrimination procedure was tested at a nominal 0.05 level for sample sizes from 10 to 50; the paper reports good Type-I error control and increasing power as sample size grows, with Weibull versus gamma the hardest comparison. For aircraft Plane 7913, which has 27 inter-failure times, the fitted Weibull model gave a geometric ratio estimate of 0.986, shape estimate of 1.135, and scale estimate of 2.750; the test did not reject Weibull against either exponential or gamma at the 0.05 level. At cycle 9, the point and upper-bound replacement strategies had reliabilities of 0.912 and 0.670 and cost rates of 12.705 and 13.767, respectively, illustrating that modest cost differences can accompany materially different risk profiles.

key_equations.name: Geometric-process cycle distribution
key_equations.explanation: F_i is the cumulative distribution function for the inter-failure time in cycle i, F is the baseline cumulative distribution function, a is the geometric ratio, i is the cycle index, and x is elapsed time.

key_equations.name: Weibull one-cycle optimal replacement age
key_equations.explanation: Tau_i* is the one-cycle optimal replacement age in cycle i, eta and m are the Weibull scale and shape parameters, a is the geometric ratio, and C_f and C_p are the corrective and preventive replacement costs.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not give a formal limitations section. They note that early-cycle failure records are short, that baseline distributions can be difficult to distinguish with limited data, and that the Weibull procedure requires numerical sampling rather than a direct pivotal construction.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The model assumes independent inter-failure times linked across cycles by a single geometric ratio, so more complex dependence or changing degradation patterns may not be represented. The case study’s maintenance conclusions are based on one aircraft, while the simulations use data generated under the assumed models; the paper does not report prospective validation across fleets or operational settings.
narrate.future_work_unstated: The framework could be tested on additional operational datasets and extended to include aircraft, usage, repair-quality, or environmental covariates that may explain differences between units. Further work could also evaluate decisions under practical maintenance windows, risk constraints, and system-level consequences, and validate the resulting policies prospectively.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for estimating reliability-oriented Shapley effects when inputs may be correlated and the number of inputs is large. It uses a sample of failed cases from a preceding reliability analysis, estimates conditional input densities, and combines closed target Sobol indices over sampled permutations. The method also estimates uncertainty using the same failure sample, avoiding additional evaluations of the model. The authors study simulated examples, including a 30-input Gaussian linear model, a 10-input fire-spread model, and adaptive importance-sampling examples for a toy function and a finance model. They find that the approach can be applied in higher dimensions, but its accuracy depends strongly on density estimation and can fall short of reference values in the fire-spread example.
narrate.key_results: In the 30-input Gaussian linear example, estimates of the tested closed target Sobol indices roughly stabilized with about 5,000 to 6,000 failed samples; splitting the sample about equally between density fitting and expectation estimation was most stable in the reported experiment. For the 30-input example, the Gaussian mixture model was reported as the most precise of the three density estimators, while kernel density estimation produced very wide intervals and normalizing flows struggled with large Shapley effects; their computation times were 1:25:45, 00:56:04, and 26:15:20, respectively. In the 10-input fire-spread example, all three density estimators produced similar estimates, but their results did not reach the reference values. The authors report that resampling captured closed-index uncertainty fairly accurately in the Gaussian example, though it could underestimate uncertainty; Shapley-effect intervals could also be conservative.

key_equations.name: Closed target Sobol index from conditional densities
key_equations.explanation: T with subscript u and superscript c is the closed target Sobol index, p with subscript t is the failure probability at threshold t, X with subscript u is the input group, F with subscript t is the failure event, the two f terms are its conditional and unconditional densities, and E is expectation under the conditional distribution.

key_equations.name: Shapley-effect aggregation
key_equations.explanation: The estimated target Shapley effect for input i averages its marginal contribution over M sampled permutations; P_i is the set of inputs preceding i in permutation pi, and each estimated T with superscript c is a closed target Sobol index.

key_equations.name: Reported permutation-sampling error bound
key_equations.explanation: The error tolerance epsilon for input i is bounded using the confidence parameter delta, the estimated universal range of its marginal contributions r, and the number M of sampled permutations.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify the lack of general theoretical guarantees for the conditional density estimates as the main limitation; density-estimation error can bias the resulting indices. Their error procedure quantifies variation around the estimator's mean, not necessarily error from the true Shapley effect, because density-estimation bias may remain. They also note that resampling may underestimate uncertainty and that their permutation-based error bounds can be wide.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The stated probability bound assumes independent marginal contributions and uses ranges estimated from a finite set of resampled estimates; this can make its claimed coverage less secure than the formula suggests. The demonstrations are simulation-based, and the fire-spread example uses a specified dependence structure rather than field observations, so performance under real operating data and more complex dependence remains untested. Repeatedly fitting densities for many input groups and permutations may also be costly as dimension and sample size increase.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose improving permutation selection, for example with quasi-Monte Carlo or importance sampling, and adapting the error procedure to those sampling methods. They also propose theoretical analysis using density estimators with tractable error properties and propagating density-estimation error into the final estimates.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the method on field reliability data and across changing operating conditions and covariates, including cases where several failure mechanisms compete. It would also be useful to assess how component-level Shapley effects support system-level risk decisions and maintenance prioritization.

narrate.summary: Slender fiber-reinforced polymer-reinforced concrete (FRP-RC) columns can fail through concrete crushing or loss of stability, and a finite-element analysis returns only the capacity of the mode that governs. The paper develops an active-learning Kriging-assisted Monte Carlo simulation (AK-MCS) method with a separate surrogate branch for each failure mode, combining their predictions by taking the lower capacity. The method is tested using simulated finite-element outputs for a study of 84 column configurations, with detailed examples covering mixed failure and cases dominated by one mode. In mixed-failure examples, many training points lie close to the transition between modes, while the design-point estimates and direct simulation results agree closely. The authors note that the approach is currently limited to two failure modes and that its applicability across the full design space remains under study.
narrate.key_results: For the two mixed-failure examples, 79% and 62% of training points were within one predictive standard deviation of the mode boundary. The first-order reliability method design-point estimates differed from the Monte Carlo estimates by 0.047 and 0.036, respectively, both within 0.05. Finite-element checks at the design points differed from the surrogate predictions by at most 0.58%. For a rare-event example, importance sampling estimated a reliability index of 6.187 with a 0.8% coefficient of variation using 2.5 × 10^5 samples, while direct simulation with 10^7 samples found no failures.

key_equations.name: Two-branch combined surrogate
key_equations.explanation: The combined predicted limit state g-hat at input vector x is the smaller of the predicted material-failure branch g-mat and predicted stability-failure branch g-stab.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the method is limited to two failure modes; a third branch may be needed where concrete crushing and FRP rupture compete. They also note that the axis-aligned training-data boxes do not prevent extrapolation in empty corners, and that the fixed importance-sampling density may miss a failure region far from its sampling centers.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated outputs from a representative column model, not field or experimental reliability data, so performance on real structures is unverified. The detailed numerical checks cover a small set of illustrative configurations, and the results may depend on the chosen input distributions and the assumptions embodied in this particular finite-element model.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors say ongoing work will investigate whether a third branch is needed for competing concrete crushing and FRP rupture, and whether a single surrogate can match the two-branch method. They also identify ongoing work to test generalization across the full design space and whether the method can replace a finite-element-based Level III reliability analysis.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Validate the predictions and uncertainty bounds against experiments and field data across different column geometries, reinforcement types, and operating conditions. Further work could also assess correlated input variables and system-level failure consequences, and use reliability estimates to support design or inspection decisions.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for combining independent experiments that use step-stress accelerated life testing (SSALT) but inspect units periodically, so failure times are known only to lie between inspections. It models the experiments with a shared proportional hazards (PH) lifetime distribution and a log-linear relationship between stress and failure rate, while allowing different stress paths, sample sizes, and inspection schedules. The method estimates reliability at the normal operating condition (NOC), mean time to failure (MTTF), and lifetime quantiles using maximum likelihood and asymptotic confidence intervals. It is evaluated using simulations, two simulated-data examples, and two laboratory tests of light-emitting diodes (LEDs). Pooling the LED tests improved precision, while the simulations showed that choosing the wrong lifetime distribution can substantially distort tail quantiles.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with exponential, Weibull, and Burr XII lifetimes and total sample sizes of 150, 300, and 450, estimates were generally close to their true values, and nearly all reported confidence-interval coverage probabilities were within the stated Monte Carlo band of 0.936 to 0.964. In the LED analysis, pooling the tests reduced the root mean squared error (RMSE) for reliability at 5 hours by 20.7% and for the 0.10 lifetime quantile by 65.8%, compared with Experiment I, the more useful single test for these measures. Coverage for reliability at 5 hours was 0.958 pooled versus 0.977 for Experiment I; coverage for the 0.10 quantile improved from 0.911 to 0.942. Under distribution misspecification, median relative bias remained within about 6%, but tail-quantile relative bias reached about 34% and changed little when sample size increased from 150 to 300.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses a numerical danger in computing ordered lower confidence limits for system reliability: a feasible optimization point gives an upper bound on the ideal endpoint, so reporting it as the lower limit can overstate reliability. It develops a cell-based computation that bounds reliability and tail probabilities over parameter regions, allowing the reported lower endpoint to remain conservative at every completed checkpoint. The framework covers general observation models, nuisance parameters, and dependence, while the implemented numerical method uses monotone binomial models. The numerical study uses four constructed binomial examples, with complete enumeration of outcomes for selected parameter values; it does not evaluate the proposed continuous-model and simulation-based extensions. The method reached its target numerical width in all four examples, and its certified all-success limit was higher than a Bonferroni-adjusted component-product limit.
narrate.key_results: All four benchmark problems reached a certified width of 10 to the power of negative 5 or less: the required subdivision counts were 17 for the scalar case, 184 for the all-success case, 1617 for the interior case, and 2904 for the partial-failure case. For the all-success observation, the certified lower limit was 0.68128, compared with 0.41738 from the Bonferroni-adjusted component-product limit; for partial failures, the respective limits were 0.31508 and 0.14362. Additional stochastic candidate searches did not change the final endpoints or subdivision counts and increased computation time in every example. Complete enumeration gave coverage of 0.94078532 at true component reliabilities 0.7 and 0.8, and coverage of 1 at each of the other two tested parameter vectors, (0.8, 0.9) and (0.9, 0.95), for the nominal 0.90 level.

narrate.limitations_stated: The numerical evaluation covers the exact monotone-binomial implementation on four scalar and two-component problems; the nonmonotone, continuous-model, censoring, and simulation-based constructions are presented theoretically but are not evaluated in those experiments. The authors identify dimension as the main unresolved computational constraint, noting the storage and subdivision costs of dense binomial Bernstein representations.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical benchmarks are low-dimensional binomial examples rather than field reliability data, and complete coverage enumeration is reported for only three true parameter vectors. As a result, the experiments do not establish practical scalability or performance for larger networks, dependent component states, or censored lifetime data, despite the broader theory covering some of these settings.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating path and cut representations, factorable relaxations, and sharper probability-distance bounds to reduce the work per retained region. They also identify allocation of simulation samples across cells and evaluation on bridge networks and censored lifetime data as next computational studies.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method on field or life-test data, including comparison of predicted confidence limits with independently established system reliability. Further work could also test models with dependent component failures and operating-condition covariates, and assess how system-level decisions change when limits are computed at different numerical widths.

narrate.summary: This perspective paper explains how reliability engineering can be adapted to artificial intelligence systems, whose failures may involve incorrect outputs, unsafe actions, poor memory handling, or failures across interacting agents. It proposes defining the failure, operating conditions, and supporting evidence together, then analyzing failure modes and measuring performance across system components, operational loops, agent conduct, and network or governance effects. It recommends matching statistical methods to the evidence, using testing before deployment, monitoring in operation, and corrective-action processes to refresh reliability evidence. The paper illustrates this approach with adversarial tests of an image classifier, simulated error propagation in vehicle perception modules, and field records of autonomous-vehicle disengagements. The field analysis uses mileage-adjusted event counts and shows that accounting for exposure and overdispersion can change conclusions about reliability growth.
narrate.key_results: The California field case covers 479 disengagements for four manufacturers from December 2017 through November 2019, with monthly mileage used as exposure. The estimated monthly changes in events per mile were minus 0.021 for Waymo, minus 0.072 for Cruise, minus 0.146 for Pony AI, and plus 0.008 for Zoox. After adjusting standard errors for overdispersion, Cruise and Pony AI had negative slopes whose intervals excluded zero; Waymo’s slope was not distinguishable from zero, and Zoox remained essentially flat. The paper also reports Pearson dispersion estimates of 2.03 for Waymo, 1.09 for Cruise, 2.99 for Pony AI, and 1.12 for Zoox; it presents the classifier and perception studies as illustrations rather than reporting new comparative performance results for them.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that detailed field-test data are difficult to obtain and are often held by industry. They note that the autonomous-vehicle monthly aggregation omits vehicle heterogeneity, that quasi-Poisson variance adjustment does not explain the overdispersion, that the Zoox trend is weakly identified because of short exposure, and that disengagements are an imperfect surrogate for hazardous behavior. They also state that controlled agent studies using simulated tasks or constructed faults need field validation before they can support failure-rate estimates.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper is a perspective and tutorial rather than a direct empirical validation of its proposed program for deployed tool-using or multi-agent systems. In the field case, manufacturer-level trends may reflect changes in routes, fleet composition, or operating conditions as well as changes in system reliability, so the reported slopes alone cannot attribute improvement to a particular corrective action.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for a field repository that links failures to exposure, operating context, versions, tools, memory, policy settings, system configuration, agent connections, reasoning traces, severity, and corrective actions. They also propose linking controlled tests with field repositories to support drift-aware reliability-growth and failure-propagation models, and encourage industry to share more detailed field data with researchers.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be prospective field studies that test whether specific safeguards, such as independent action gates or memory controls, reduce exposure-adjusted failures under defined operating conditions. The framework could also be extended to quantify how different failure mechanisms combine at the system level and to guide decisions about when to automate, require human confirmation, or stop deployment.

narrate.summary: This review addresses the computational burden of estimating reliability and risk measures when high-fidelity simulations are expensive, especially for rare failures and extreme outcomes. It describes methods that combine models of different costs and accuracy to estimate the high-fidelity model's probability of failure, tail severity, and buffered probability of failure more efficiently. The methods covered are control variates, importance sampling, and active learning with probabilistic surrogate models. The paper is a methodological review rather than a new experiment: it uses no original dataset, and its precision-oncology example is illustrative. Its central message is that lower-fidelity models can reduce the need for expensive evaluations while preserving accuracy when they provide useful information about the target risk quantity.
narrate.key_results: The review reports no new numerical benchmark, estimation-accuracy result, or measured cost comparison. It states that multifidelity approaches have achieved reductions of orders of magnitude in computational cost without compromising accuracy, and explains that the benefit depends on model cost and the statistical relationship between model outputs. It notes that conventional Monte Carlo can require thousands or more high-fidelity evaluations to estimate tail quantities accurately. The review compares three methodological strategies conceptually: reduce estimator variance, concentrate evaluations in rare-event regions, or adaptively select informative locations and model fidelities.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify open problems in extending multifidelity methods to optimization under uncertainty, including allocating computation across design points, uncertain inputs, and model fidelities, and estimating risk gradients. They also state that efficient multifidelity acquisition functions tailored to tail measures such as conditional value-at-risk remain to be developed, and that useful model hierarchies require application-specific domain expertise.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The review presents no common numerical benchmark or original validation, so its broad claims of large cost reductions cannot be assessed across the methods it surveys. Practical performance also depends on relationships between models and, for importance sampling, on a sampling distribution that covers the full support of the nominal input distribution; the review does not quantify how robust the methods are when those conditions are poorly estimated.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing multifidelity methods for optimization under uncertainty, including better joint allocation of resources across design space, input space, and fidelities, and efficient estimation of risk gradients. They call for information reuse across repeated analyses, application-aware frameworks that integrate physical knowledge and data, and new acquisition functions designed for tail measures. They also describe potential use in digital twins for aerospace, energy, and precision medicine.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare the three method classes on shared reliability test problems, reporting accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and computational cost under consistent budgets. They could also validate predictions against field or operational data and test how dependence among uncertain inputs, model discrepancy, and changing operating conditions affect rare-event estimates.

narrate.summary: Incomplete and inconsistent reliability records from different sources can make failure-rate estimates uncertain and inconsistent across facility studies. The paper presents a procedure that selects relevant records, models each failure rate with a Gamma distribution under a constant failure-rate assumption, and combines distributions for the same equipment. It tests two combination methods using simulated data and applies them to operational reliability information for selected accelerator equipment at the International Fusion Materials Irradiation Facility–Demo Oriented Neutron Energy Source (IFMIF-DONES). The real-data application uses records from the Fusion Component Failure Rate Database (FCFRDB), including interface flanges, pumps, transformers, amplifiers, compressors, and sensors. The main finding is that moment matching is efficient when sources are homogeneous, while minimizing Kullback–Leibler divergence is preferable when heterogeneity is present or uncertain.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with a target Gamma distribution having shape 3 and scale 1.5, the homogeneous case with 5 studies produced estimated shape and scale values of 3.029 and 1.494 by moment matching, and 3.044 and 1.487 by the divergence method. Under the heterogeneous case with 5 studies, the corresponding estimates were 1.709 and 3.147 for moment matching, and 2.143 and 2.511 for the divergence method; with 500 studies they improved to 2.928 and 1.541, and 2.975 and 1.517, respectively. In a simulation based on interface-flange data, the target shape and scale were 0.718 and 3.813 × 10⁻⁶; with 500 heterogeneous studies, the estimates were 0.696 and 3.913 × 10⁻⁶ by moments and 0.706 and 3.860 × 10⁻⁶ by divergence. For the real-data application, the combined interface-flange distributions were Gamma with shape 0.157 and scale 8.419 × 10⁻⁶ by moments, and shape 0.316 and scale 4.173 × 10⁻⁶ by divergence; the paper reports no separate predictive-error or runtime measurements.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the application had too few studies per component to distinguish failure modes when combining data, so they combined information without separating those modes. They also note that residual differences between sources can remain despite expert screening, and that the application assigns equal weights to the source distributions.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The constant failure-rate assumption may not represent equipment with aging, wear-out, or changing operating conditions. The simulations use constructed distributions, and the operational-data application does not validate the combined distributions against an independent set of observed failure histories or future outcomes. Equal source weights may also give the same influence to records with different data quality or relevance.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose separating failure modes in future applications when sufficient data are available, and examining alternative ways to assign mixture weights, including expert-based, optimization-based, or hierarchical Bayesian approaches. They also identify application to a substantially larger dataset from the EUROfusion Early Neutron Source Work Package as a valuable next step.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test the method with time-varying failure rates and explicit covariates such as operating conditions, while accounting for censored exposure and differences in data quality. Prospective validation against field failure histories and assessment of how alternative aggregated distributions affect maintenance and spare-parts decisions would help establish operational performance.

narrate.summary: The paper studies how many failures are needed to tell whether a finite population of failure-producing units is being depleted, rather than behaving like an inexhaustible source. It models independent time-to-failure observations whose rates decline as units fail, with unknown rate parameters and, in an extension, unknown trends in detection effort. The main example is the Jelinski–Moranda (JM) software reliability model; a second example allows a linear trend in log effort. The analysis uses theoretical likelihood results and simulations of synthetic exponential failure times, not field data. It finds that fitting nuisance trends can remove the leading depletion signal and increase the number of failures needed for detection.
narrate.key_results: With an unknown common failure-rate level, the finite-versus-infinite population boundary occurs when the number of observed failures grows on the order of the population size to the two-thirds power. When an unknown linear effort trend is also fitted, the first depletion trend is absorbed and the boundary moves to the four-fifths power. At the boundary, the probability that the maximum likelihood estimate of population size is infinite approaches Φ of negative h; under the exact infinite-population model that probability is one half. In the JM simulation at scale coefficient 2, the reported profile log-likelihood ratio had simulated mean 0.35 and variance 0.71, compared with limiting values 0.33 and 0.67. For the effort-trend simulations, the feasible and oracle tests made the same decision in more than 99% of replicates.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the two-parameter effort-drift example has no counterpart to the JM exact criterion for an infinite estimate, and its profile likelihood is not available in closed form. They also describe the fractional-order boundary for a heavy-tailed latent-rate example as a conjecture whose proof is beyond the paper’s scope.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The conclusions rely on independent failure times and specified parametric rate trends; departures such as dependent failures or multiple failure mechanisms are not evaluated. The evidence for the effort-drift case is simulation-based, and the paper provides no validation on observed software or other field failure data. Its asymptotic detection boundaries also concern sparse depletion and may not describe experiments outside that regime.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying how thinning, aggregation, interior censoring, and marginalization affect the order of the observable depletion signal. They also conjecture that a fractional-order boundary may apply to removal experiments with heavy-tailed latent rates and leave its proof for future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the boundaries using field failure-time data and to assess robustness to dependence, changing operating conditions, and competing failure mechanisms. Further work could also connect the confidence sets that may include an infinite population to practical decisions about testing effort, maintenance, or software release.

narrate.summary: This perspective paper explains how reliability engineering can be applied to artificial intelligence systems, whose failures can include unsound reasoning, unsafe actions, persistent memory errors, and failures among interacting agents. It proposes defining the system’s operating envelope and failure severity, analyzing failure modes, selecting measures suited to the data, and using testing, deployment monitoring, and corrective-action processes to refresh reliability evidence. The framework is illustrated with California public-road autonomous-vehicle disengagement and mileage records, a laboratory classifier test under adversarial input, and simulated errors in vehicle-perception modules. The authors find that established reliability methods remain useful, but require AI-specific failure definitions, exposure records, and attention to overdispersion and dependence. They conclude that reliable field assessment of autonomous agents is constrained by the lack of longitudinal operational data with exposure and system context.
narrate.key_results: The California case analyzed 479 disengagements across Waymo, Cruise, Pony AI, and Zoox from December 2017 through November 2019, using monthly mileage as exposure. Reported rates per 1,000 miles were 0.083 for Waymo, 0.120 for Cruise, 0.225 for Pony AI, and 0.593 for Zoox. Estimated monthly log-rate slopes were −0.021 for Waymo, −0.072 for Cruise, −0.146 for Pony AI, and +0.008 for Zoox; after adjusting standard errors for overdispersion, Cruise and Pony AI showed evidence of declining events per mile, while Waymo’s slope was not distinguishable from zero and Zoox remained flat. The laboratory and simulation cases illustrate reliability-growth and dependent-error methods, but the paper reports no numerical comparison establishing that one method or control outperforms another.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the California analysis aggregates data by manufacturer and month, omitting vehicle-level heterogeneity, and that quasi-Poisson variance adjustment does not explain the overdispersion. They note that Zoox has short exposure, that disengagements are a human-gated surrogate that can miss hazardous behavior without a takeover, and that collisions should not be pooled with disengagements without a severity model. They also identify the lack of granular, longitudinal field records for agents and the difficulty of obtaining proprietary industry data.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The three examples do not constitute a field validation of the proposed program for tool-using or multi-agent systems; the agent-related evidence is largely conceptual, laboratory-based, or simulated. The manufacturer-level trends also cannot by themselves establish that a particular reliability intervention caused improvement, since the analysis does not isolate changes in operating conditions or other concurrent changes.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for field repositories that record exposure, operating context, system configuration, tools, memory, policies, agent connections, reasoning traces, outcomes, and corrective actions. They propose linking controlled testing to field observations, validating failure mechanisms in deployment, and expanding industry–academic data-sharing initiatives.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be prospective evaluation of specific safeguards, with consistent measures of prevented harm, false alarms, recovery, and human-review burden across deployments. Studies could also assess how reliability evidence should guide deployment or autonomy decisions when failure severity and the costs of intervention differ across applications.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses uncertainty in Weibull lifetime and reliability estimates when a life test ends at a fixed time, so some units have only right-censored lifetimes. It develops generalized confidence intervals for Weibull shape, scale, and reliability using least-squares probability-plot estimators and a transformation from Weibull lifetimes to a Gumbel location–scale model. For censored samples, it uses the observed number of failures and generated uniform order statistics, and solves an estimating equation for the probability of failure by the censoring time. The method is evaluated in simulations and illustrated with complete ball-bearing data and a public dataset with Type-I censoring. The proposed intervals usually have coverage near the nominal level in the scenarios studied, although their lengths vary and can be large.
narrate.key_results: The simulations used 2,000 replications per scenario and 1,000 generalized pivotal quantity draws per interval; censored scenarios covered target censoring proportions of 20%, 30%, and 50%. For shape intervals, the proposed method’s coverage was generally close to 0.95 at 20% and 30% censoring, but fell to about 0.88–0.94 in several 50% censoring settings with sample size 20. For reliability near one, with shape 5 and scale 5, coverage at 50% censoring and sample size 20 was 0.925 and 0.896 for the two plotting estimators at time 1.2, compared with 0.924 and 0.928 at sample size 50. The comparison methods showed different coverage–length trade-offs; for example, at sample size 50, shape 2, scale 2, and 20% censoring, the proposed scale interval had coverage 0.965 and average length 9.884, while the least-squares bootstrap had coverage 0.950 and average length 0.908. In the public censored example, 10 of 20 units failed before time 500, and the fitted methods did not reject the Weibull model at the 5% level.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that each generalized pivotal quantity draw requires numerical root finding for the auxiliary failure probability, which can be computationally intensive. The censored-data construction also requires at least two observed failures and assumes that its estimating equation has a unique solution under the stated regularity conditions.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method assumes a two-parameter Weibull lifetime model and the simulations examine only a limited set of parameter values and censoring levels, so performance under other failure-time distributions or mechanisms is not established. The two examples provide illustrations, but the paper does not validate the procedure across broader field datasets, operating conditions, covariates, or dependent system-level failures.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could assess the method under competing failure mechanisms, covariates, changing operating conditions, and dependent component or system lifetimes. Validation on larger field datasets and evaluation of how interval estimates support maintenance or risk decisions would also be useful.

narrate.summary: This theory paper studies reliability comparisons for series and parallel systems whose independent component lifetimes follow the Exponentiated Gumbel Type-II distribution (EG2). It models component lifetimes with a three-parameter distribution and uses majorization of the parameters to derive comparisons between the minimum and maximum component lifetimes. The work uses no lifetime data and does not estimate parameters or optimize a design; numerical examples illustrate some theoretical results. A central finding is that majorization can give useful orderings for series systems, but it does not generally give a usual stochastic ranking for parallel-system lifetimes when inner shape parameters vary. The paper also shows that series-system failure rates have a proportional relationship under common scale and inner shape parameters, whereas parallel-system failure rates generally do not.
narrate.key_results: For series systems with common scale and inner shape parameters, the paper establishes usual stochastic, likelihood-ratio, mean residual life, increasing convex, star, and dispersive orderings under the stated parameter conditions; the likelihood-ratio comparison is equivalent to an inequality between the sums of the outer shape parameters. The lowest order statistic has a proportional failure-rate relationship, but the highest order statistic generally does not; in the illustration with outer-shape vectors (1, 3) and (2, 2), the parallel-system failure-rate ratio starts at approximately 0.75 and declines toward 0.50 over the displayed range from 0 to 10. The paper establishes reversed failure-rate ordering for the highest order statistic under majorization of outer shape parameters, and usual stochastic ordering for the lowest order statistic under majorization of inner shape parameters. For joint variation in scale and outer shape parameters, it gives usual stochastic order results for both system types under specified chain-majorization conditions, while an example shows that reliability curves for parallel systems can cross under inner-shape heterogeneity.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their results rely on independence and structural parameter restrictions, including equality of selected parameters and membership of parameter vectors or matrices in specified sets. They note that these conditions ensure the majorization arguments and should be regarded as sufficient rather than necessary.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The conclusions are mathematical comparisons under idealized assumptions, not validated estimates of reliability for an operating system; the paper provides no field-data validation or uncertainty assessment for fitted parameters. The numerical examples illustrate selected cases and do not establish how robust the comparisons are outside the stated parameter conditions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the results to more general parameter settings. They also suggest studying dependent component lifetimes, including copula-based dependence, and more complex configurations such as k-out-of-n systems.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could assess the ordering results using field or accelerated-life data, including tests of whether the EG2 model and its assumptions fit actual component lifetimes. It could also examine competing failure mechanisms and operating-condition covariates, and connect the comparisons to system-level design or maintenance decisions.

narrate.summary: Structural reliability analysis can be difficult for engineers without specialist expertise, and errors in problem formulation or method choice can lead to inaccurate failure estimates. The paper presents a multi-agent framework that converts natural-language descriptions of component-level structural problems into a structured model, selects an analysis category, generates solver code, executes it, and interprets the results. Numerical reliability estimates come from deterministic execution of reliability solvers rather than being generated by a language model. The method planner is trained on 150 synthetic examples to choose among first-order reliability methods, Monte Carlo simulation, and advanced sampling methods. The framework was evaluated on 20 hand-authored benchmark problems and generally agreed more closely with reference estimates than direct language-model answers, although some method choices produced large errors.
narrate.key_results: The framework generated executable analyses and parseable estimates for all 20 held-out benchmark problems. Its median relative error in failure probability was 3.8%, compared with 76.6% for direct answers from a single language model; errors exceeded 50% in 2 problems for the framework and 12 for the direct answers. Fine-tuning the planner produced 65% exact method-category accuracy, compared with 40% for the smaller untuned model and 50% for the larger untuned model; its acceptable-selection rate was 70%, compared with 40% and 50%. In the end-to-end comparison, mean relative error was 17.20% with the fine-tuned planner and 52.51% with the untuned planner, which did not return an estimate for one of the 20 problems. Important exceptions included a strongly nonlinear case where the framework’s reliability index was 3.03 against a reference of 2.00, and a rare-event case where its failure probability was 1.2 × 10⁻⁹ against a reference of 9.3 × 10⁻⁹.

key_equations.name: Failure probability
key_equations.explanation: The probability of failure P_f is the integral of the joint density f_X(x) over values x of the random-variable vector X for which the limit-state function g(X) is zero or less.

key_equations.name: Reliability index
key_equations.explanation: The reliability index beta is the negative inverse standard normal cumulative distribution function Phi applied to the probability of failure P_f.

narrate.limitations_stated: The evaluation uses only 20 held-out, hand-authored benchmark problems, limiting statistical precision and generalization; the observed differences in method-selection accuracy were not statistically significant at the 0.05 level. The framework is limited to component-level problems whose limit-state functions can be evaluated directly in generated code, and the refinement offer was not evaluated in the benchmark.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The benchmark does not establish performance on field problems or on models coupled to real structural analysis software, so real-world input quality and solver integration remain untested. Because the reference labels use an expert-defined threshold rule and the same rule is used to assess the planner, the reported selection accuracy measures agreement with that rule rather than independent engineering suitability.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose adding system-reliability methods, linking the framework to finite-element solvers, accepting multimodal inputs, expanding the benchmark to real-world cases, and increasing training data and the set of selectable methods. They also propose retrieving probabilistic models and target reliability levels from authoritative standards using retrieval-augmented generation, and comparing the planner with closed-source language models and classical classifiers.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future evaluation could test the complete workflow on field-derived structural cases and independently review whether extracted variables, dependence assumptions, and limit states match engineering records. The authors could also assess how uncertainty in user-provided distributions and dependence affects method choice and final estimates, and measure the computational cost of each workflow option.
